note: Version 3.1: Anthropological verification applied. Corrected 17 anachronisms (post-Columbian foods mislabeled as ancestral), dating errors, and regional inaccuracies. Chili peppers, tomatoes, potatoes, cassava, peanuts, and maize flagged where introduced post-1492. Enhanced with 34 additional genetic variants from December 2025 research. Includes caffeine metabolism (CYP1A2), celiac risk (HLA-DQ), cholesterol (APOE, PCSK9), micronutrient variants, and bitter taste perception (TAS2R38). AMY1 copy numbers adjusted per Bolognini 2024 digital PCR methodology. Version 3.2: Added 5 new dietary regions (nile_valley, mesopotamian, caribbean_creole, mestizo_mesoamerican, malagasy) for improved geographic accuracy. Genetic adaptations placeholders included for future research.

cultures.diet_signature: Hunter-gatherer diet featuring native seeds, bush fruits, and game adapted to arid conditions. Emphasizes seasonal availability, fire-stick farming, and diverse protein from land and sea.

Rainforest diet featuring cassava, river fish, and wild game. Archaeological evidence shows maize agriculture from ~4850 BCE (6,850 years ago) based on phytolith analysis, alongside cassava cultivation. Emphasizes fermented beverages, insects, and diverse tropical fruits with slash-and-burn agriculture.
Bridge between Mediterranean and Central Asian cuisines featuring grilled meats, yogurt, and stuffed vegetables. Emphasizes olive oil, bulgur, and mezze traditions.
High-altitude agriculture featuring diverse potato varieties, quinoa, and camelid herding. Includes freeze-dried chuño, guinea pig, and adaptations to low-oxygen conditions.
Desert-adapted diet centered on dates, camel products, and preserved foods. Features rice dishes with lamb, minimal vegetables, and hospitality-focused preparation.

Australian coastal Aboriginal peoples developed sophisticated marine harvesting practices over 65,000 years. Rock oysters, fish, shellfish, and estuarine resources formed the protein base, complemented by coastal plants, seeds, and seasonal inland game. The diet was sustainable, seasonal, and highly nutritious with excellent omega-3 fatty acid profiles from marine foods.

modern_substitutes.Kangaroo/Emu: Grass-fed beef or lamb (though kangaroo is commercially available)

cultures.diet_signature: Ottoman-era (14th century+) fusion of Turkish, Mediterranean, and Slavic traditions. Signature dishes like ćevapi and burek arrived with Ottoman influence—ćevapi first documented in Belgrade in the 1860s, burek spread after the 1350s. Pre-Ottoman Balkan diet centered on wheat, barley, millet, pork, and sheep. Features grilled meats, yogurt, phyllo pastries, and fermented vegetables.
Delta cuisine centered on freshwater fish, rice, and mustard oil. Features five-spice blends, minimal heat spicing, and delicate fish preparations with mustard paste.

Brazilian coastal cuisine, especially from Bahia, represents a vibrant fusion of African, Indigenous, and Portuguese influences. Characterized by dendê (red palm oil), coconut milk, cassava/manioc, and abundant seafood. The African influence is strong in cooking techniques and ingredient combinations, creating distinctive dishes unlike other South American cuisines.

modern_substitutes.Dendê oil: Combination of palm oil and paprika for color

cultures.diet_signature: California coastal indigenous peoples developed sophisticated food systems centered on acorn processing, salmon runs, and marine resources. Acorns were leached and ground into flour, complemented by abundant shellfish, salmon, seeds, and game. The diet was remarkably diverse with seasonal variation and included extensive use of native plant foods.

The Canadian Prairies diet represents a fusion of Plains indigenous foodways and Subarctic influences. Bison was the primary protein source, preserved as pemmican for winter survival. Wild rice harvested from lakes, berries, and root vegetables supplemented the meat-heavy diet. The harsh climate required high-fat, nutrient-dense foods that could be stored long-term.

Afro-Caribbean fusion cuisine born from the colonial era (16th-19th century), blending West African, European, and Indigenous Taino foodways. Characterized by rice and peas, jerk seasonings, tropical fruits, and seafood. Distinct from indigenous Taino diet—incorporates African okra, plantains, and salted fish brought via the slave trade, plus European livestock and seasonings.

modern_substitutes.saltfish: fresh cod or other white fish

cultures.diet_signature: Island tropical diet centered on maize, cassava, and sweet potato with abundant seafood. Archaeological starch grain assemblages show maize was more prominent than previously assumed, with cassava showing minimal presence in some contexts. Features cassava bread, tropical fruits, and simple preparations adapted to island resources.
Mountain cuisine featuring walnuts, herbs, fermented dairy, and grilled meats. Emphasizes fresh cheeses, wild greens, and stone-baked breads with liberal use of aromatic herbs.
Hunter-gatherer diet from rainforest resources including wild yams, fish, insects, and game. Seasonal variety with minimal processing and high biodiversity.
Nomadic pastoralist diet dominated by meat and dairy with minimal plant foods. Features fermented horse milk, boiled meats, and preserved dairy products for winter survival.

Robust grain and dairy-based cuisine featuring rye bread, beer, pork, and preserved foods. Highest lactase persistence in Europe with intense dairy traditions including fresh milk, quark, and aged cheeses. Beer culture from grain fermentation.
Robust fermented foods, hearty root vegetables, and preserved preparations for long winters. Rich in sour cream, buckwheat, and wild mushrooms with minimal refined ingredients.
Three Sisters agriculture supplemented by hunting, fishing, and foraging. Features maize, beans, and squash with maple, wild rice, and abundant game in forested regions.
Injera-based meals featuring complex spice blends, lentils, and fermented preparations. Rich in teff, berbere spice, and communal eating traditions with substantial plant-based options.

Post-colonial (16th century+) pastoral diet centered on cattle introduced by Spanish. Pre-contact Pampas indigenous diet featured guanaco, rhea, armadillo, and fish. The iconic beef-centered gaucho cuisine represents colonial-era synthesis, not deep ancestral tradition.

modern_substitutes.Organ meats: Grass-fed beef cuts for those unfamiliar

cultures.diet_signature: Bison-centered nomadic diet with high fat content. Protein limited to ~35% of calories due to protein toxicity ceiling (rabbit starvation)—required substantial fat supplementation and plant foods (roots, berries, prairie turnips) for nutritional balance. Features pemmican (dried meat + fat) for preservation and complete utilization of buffalo.
Mountain agricultural diet featuring upland rice, foraged greens, and simple preparations. Emphasizes sticky rice, fermented foods, and limited spicing with pork as primary meat.
Nomadic and coastal diet featuring camel products, sorghum flatbreads, and fresh seafood. Incorporates dates, spices from trade routes, and minimal vegetable content.

Extreme cold-adapted marine mammal-based diet with 50-75% fat from blubber. Contrary to popular belief, NOT ketogenic—marine glycogen, fermented foods, kelp, and seasonal plants provided 15-20% carbohydrates. Features raw and fermented preparations with protein limited to 25-35% to avoid protein toxicity (rabbit starvation). Vitamin C obtained from raw organ meats (muktuk/whale skin, liver) and kelp. Note: Marine mammals contain significant glycogen (8-30% carbs in blubber), providing 15-20% of calories as carbohydrates—diet was not ketogenic as sometimes claimed.
Minimalist cuisine emphasizing seasonal ingredients, fermentation, and umami. Features rice, seafood, seaweed, and soy with meticulous preparation and presentation.
Fermentation-focused cuisine featuring kimchi, doenjang, and gochugaru. Emphasizes banchan diversity, communal eating, and balanced flavors with substantial seafood.
Mountain cuisine featuring wild greens, yogurt, and grilled meats. Emphasizes simple preparations, bulgur, and seasonal foraging with pastoral dairy traditions.

Traditional pastoralist diet centered on meat, fat, and blood from cattle with fermented dairy. Archaeological ceramic analysis reveals LOW milk residues in pottery (milk was stored in gourds/wooden vessels that don't preserve); ceramics show meat, bones, marrow, and fat processing. Ancient DNA shows only 1 in 8 East African pastoralists carried lactase persistence, suggesting fermented dairy (yogurt) was primary form. Plant foods in stews/soups consistently present in archaeological record.
Aromatic slow-cooked dishes featuring preserved ingredients, warming spices, and semolina-based staples. Balances sweet and savory with dates, nuts, and complex spice blends.

Unique Austronesian-African fusion reflecting Madagascar's settlement history (~500 CE from Indonesia/Borneo, with later African migration). Rice dominates every meal—an Austronesian trait unusual in Africa. Features zebu cattle, seafood, and tropical produce. Vanilla and coconut are signature flavors. Distinct from both Southeast Asian and mainland African cuisines.

Temperate Polynesian diet adapted to cooler climate featuring kumara, fern root, and seafood. Moa hunting caused extinction within ~100 years of arrival (~1280-1320 CE); kumara agriculture intensified as compensation. Important: pigs and chickens were NOT prehistoric in New Zealand—ancient DNA dates all specimens to 18th century European introduction. Features traditional hangi (earth-oven) cooking.
A mezze-based tradition featuring tahini, yogurt, chickpeas, and abundant fresh herbs. Combines grains with vegetables and moderate amounts of lamb or fish.
A sun-drenched cuisine centered on olive oil, seasonal vegetables, fresh fish, and whole grains. Emphasizes fermented dairy, legumes, and minimal red meat with abundant herbs and aromatic plants.
typical_dishes: pasta with olive oil and garlic

cultures.diet_signature: Tropical island diet featuring sago, root vegetables, and diverse seafood. Emphasizes earth-oven cooking, coconut preparations, and foraged greens with high carbohydrate content.

Advanced agricultural civilization diet centered on nixtamalized corn, beans, and squash. Features sophisticated use of chiles, cacao, and amaranth with insect protein and minimal dairy. Stable isotope analysis confirms C4 maize consumption comprised 50-70% of dietary carbon (Î´13C values -13.4â€° to -6.9â€°). Recent ceramic residue analysis revolutionized understanding of cacao: 56% of ALL vessels (including commoner households) contained cacao residues, overturning the elite-only assumption.

Fertile Crescent agricultural tradition—birthplace of wheat, barley, and legume cultivation (~10,000 BCE). Iraqi cuisine features slow-cooked stews, grilled meats, rice dishes, and abundant dates. Distinct from Kurdish highland cuisine—lowland river valley diet with more rice, fish, and date cultivation. Strong Persian and Arab influences.
typical_dishes: timman bagilla (rice with dill and fava)

modern_substitutes.loomi: lime zest with pinch of fermented flavor

cultures.diet_signature: Spanish-Indigenous fusion cuisine developed after 1521 conquest. Blends ancient Mesoamerican staples (corn, beans, chiles, squash) with Spanish introductions (rice, wheat, pork, beef, cheese, dairy). The mestizo diet differs from indigenous Mesoamerican by incorporating Old World livestock, dairy, and wheat alongside the native three sisters agriculture.
Small-island diet relying on breadfruit, coconut, and marine resources. Features simple preparations adapted to limited agricultural land with heavy dependence on the sea.
Extreme climate adaptation with near-exclusive reliance on animal products. Features fermented dairy, boiled meats, and milk tea with minimal grain consumption.
Mountain diet adapted across altitudes featuring millet, buckwheat, and dairy. Combines Tibetan and Indian influences with substantial yak products and hearty lentil preparations.

Ancient agricultural diet centered on the Nile River's fertile floodplain. One of humanity's oldest grain-based food systems, featuring ful medames (fava beans), bread, and river fish. Distinct from Maghreb/Berber cuisine—emphasizes legumes, alliums, and Nile fish rather than couscous and tagines. Archaeological evidence shows bread and beer production from ~4000 BCE.

Highland agriculture and lake fishing traditions featuring plantains, millet, sorghum, and freshwater fish. Diverse diet from altitude gradients with cattle herding, fishing, and highland crops. Fermented beverages and limited dairy use.
Cold-climate cuisine emphasizing preserved fish, dense rye breads, and foraged berries. Features fermented and pickled preparations with minimal processing and high omega-3 content.
Wheat-based northern cuisine featuring noodles, dumplings, and preserved vegetables. Emphasizes lamb, cabbage, and hearty flavors adapted to cold winters.
Wheat-based cuisine with complex spice combinations, dairy, and legumes. Features tandoor cooking, ghee, and substantial vegetarian options with aromatic masalas.
Salmon-rich coastal diet with abundant seafood, berries, and camas root. Features sophisticated smoking and preserving techniques with seasonal fishing traditions.
Temperate southern hemisphere diet featuring guanaco, potatoes, and coastal resources. Adapted to cool climate with seafood, wild game, and native berries.

Ancient Persian cuisine built on wheat and barley, with pomegranate, saffron, and walnuts. Rice was a 'relative newcomer'—no word appears in the Avesta, with major prominence only from the Safavid era (16th century). Features slow-cooked stews (khoresh), sweet-sour flavor profiles, and aromatic herbs.
Island cuisine centered on starchy tubers, coconut, and seafood. Features earth-oven cooking, raw fish preparations, and substantial carbohydrate content from root vegetables.
Drought-adapted cuisine based on millet, sorghum, and groundnuts. Features shea butter, dried ingredients, and pastoralist elements with high carbohydrate content.
Archipelago cuisine featuring coconut, tropical fruits, and seafood diversity. Emphasizes rice, fermented preparations, and regional spice variations across thousands of islands.
Tropical cuisine balancing sweet, sour, salty, and spicy with fish sauce, lemongrass, and coconut. Features sticky rice, fresh herbs, and abundant seafood with complex flavor layering.

Siberian diets evolved for extreme cold survival, featuring preserved and fermented foods that could last through brutal winters. Reindeer provides meat, fat, and organs while horse meat is prized. Fish is frozen raw (stroganina) or fermented. The diet is very high in fat and protein with minimal carbohydrates, supplemented by wild berries in summer.

Sichuan cuisine historically featured the numbing sensation (má) of indigenous Sichuan peppercorn. Chili peppers arrived in the 16th-17th century, adding spicy heat (là) to create the modern málà combination. Pre-chili Sichuan cooking emphasized fermented beans, ginger, and the unique tongue-numbing huājiāo.
Rice-based southern cuisine with abundant seafood, vegetables, and stir-frying. Emphasizes fresh ingredients, quick cooking, and subtle seasoning with ginger and soy.
Rice-based cuisine with coconut, tamarind, and fermented preparations. Emphasizes seafood, lentils, and complex vegetarian dishes with distinctive spice blends and curry leaves.

POST-COLONIAL FUSION (17th century+): The described cuisine emerged from African, Native American, and European synthesis after 1670s. Pre-contact Native American diet in this region featured maize, beans, squash, deer, turkey, and nuts. Rice cultivation arrived with enslaved Africans in the 1670s-1690s. This entry describes historical Southern cuisine, not deep ancestral tradition.
Maize-based porridges with wild game, insects, and indigenous plants. Combines agricultural and hunter-gatherer traditions with fermented beverages.
Desert-adapted Three Sisters agriculture with corn as centerpiece. Features blue corn, beans, squash, and chili peppers with minimal meat and sophisticated water management.
Boreal forest hunter-gatherer diet featuring caribou, moose, and fish. Adapted to long winters with preserved meats, berries, and roots with high protein and fat content.
Savanna transition zone diet between Sahel and rainforest. Features sorghum, millet, cassava, and wild game with seasonal variation. Mix of pastoral and agricultural traditions with foraged foods.
High-altitude diet centered on yak products and barley. Features butter tea, roasted flour, and preserved preparations for extreme climate with minimal vegetables.
Starchy tubers and grains paired with rich nut-based sauces and palm oil. Features fermented preparations, okra, and fish with minimal dairy and abundant plant diversity.

Western Indian cuisine spans from the vegetarian Gujarati and Rajasthani traditions to coastal Goan and Maharashtrian influences. The diet emphasizes millet and lentil combinations, extensive use of yogurt and ghee, and distinctive sweet-savory flavor profiles. Coastal areas incorporate more seafood and coconut, while interior regions favor millet-based flatbreads and preserved foods.
Hearty fare built on dairy, root vegetables, and grains adapted to cool climates. Features slow-cooked stews, fermented dairy, and preserved meats with minimal spices.
